name: BASS
experimental_objective: Determine ignition, flame spread, and extinction limits of solid spacecraft materials in microgravity under forced co-flow airflow conditions within the Microgravity Science Glovebox fan-driven duct.
fuel_material: Cotton-fiberglass composite, PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate), Nomex fabric
fuel_geometry: Thin flat sheets 10×2 cm, rod samples 10 cm length
key_findings: Microgravity flames spread slower than 1g due to absence of buoyancy-driven convection. Flame extinction occurs at higher O2 concentrations in 0g than 1g (LOC ~18% at 0g vs ~15% at 1g for cotton-fiberglass). The PMMA sheet sustained combustion down to 19% O2 at 10 cm/s airflow. At very low airflow (<3 cm/s), radiative quenching dominates and flames self-extinguish even at 25% O2.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Nomex shows best flame resistance among tested materials. Low-velocity forced ventilation below 5 cm/s creates a dangerous near-quench regime that is hard to detect. Material selection criteria for ISS and future habitats must account for 0g LOC shifts.
earth_spinoff_application: Improved flammability test standards for aircraft cabin materials (FAA burn testing methodology updated based on BASS 0g LOC data).

name: BASS-II
full_name: Burning and Suppression of Solids II
experimental_objective: Extend BASS with broader O2 range and additional materials including wire insulation; characterize extinction via CO2 and N2 dilution at reduced gravity.
fuel_material: PMMA, Nylon 6,6, Silicone rubber wire insulation, Acetal (Delrin)
fuel_geometry: Wire insulation: 10 cm segments; sheet samples 10×2 cm
key_findings: Wire insulation (silicone rubber) proved most dangerous: flames persisted down to 15.5% O2 in 0g, well below Earth-equivalent LOC. CO2 dilution raised LOC more effectively than N2 dilution per unit mole fraction. Flame standoff distance increases with O2 and decreases with airflow—a critical cue for optical fire detection algorithm tuning.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Silicone-insulated wiring presents an underappreciated ignition and propagation hazard in 0g. Recommend CO2-based inerting over N2 for cable conduit suppression in ISS-class vehicles. Optical detectors should track flame standoff not just emission intensity.
earth_spinoff_application: Wire insulation flammability rating database used by IEC 60332 standards bodies; CO2 inerting data adopted by aircraft cargo compartment suppression designers.

name: SPICE
experimental_objective: Measure the laminar smoke point of gaseous fuels (ethylene, propane, methane) in a co-flow diffusion flame at varying forced airflow velocities in 0g. Determine soot formation and smoke point height dependence on flow conditions.
fuel_geometry: Laminar co-flow burner, 1.1 mm inner diameter fuel tube, outer air tube 11 mm ID
key_findings: In 0g, smoke points are ~40% lower flame height than 1g equivalent, meaning microgravity flames produce more soot at shorter lengths due to lack of buoyancy-induced stretch. Ethylene has the lowest smoke point. Increasing co-flow reduces soot by improving oxidizer mixing but above 15 cm/s transitions to liftoff. The soot zone in 0g is a uniform annular shell unlike 1g's tip-concentrated plume.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Microgravity combustion events will produce soot earlier and more uniformly—smoke detectors must respond to lower particle concentrations than Earth-calibrated units. Fuel leak scenarios from gaseous propulsion components represent a significant unrecognized smoke source.
earth_spinoff_application: Soot formation models from SPICE data improved combustion efficiency of low-soot gas turbine combustors and informed diesel engine injector design to reduce particulate emissions.

name: SLICE
full_name: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
experimental_objective: Characterize flame liftoff, blowout, and stabilization limits of lifted diffusion flames under forced co-flow in 0g. Understand how turbulent transition and local extinction affect spacecraft fire behavior.
fuel_geometry: Co-flow burner 1.6 mm fuel tube; 11 mm air annulus
key_findings: Flame liftoff height in 0g is 20-30% greater than 1g at the same fuel jet velocity because buoyancy normally stabilizes 1g flames. Blowout velocity is 25% lower in 0g. At 25% O2, liftoff threshold is shifted to lower velocities. Stable lifted flames in microgravity can persist at conditions where 1g flames would attach—increasing standoff and masking detection.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Ventilation fans creating local air velocities above 20 cm/s may inadvertently lift and stabilize diffusion flames from leaking fuel lines rather than extinguishing them. Cabin airflow design must account for liftoff stabilization in 0g.
earth_spinoff_application: Liftoff data fed into industrial burner stabilization models for natural gas furnaces; improved safety cutoff algorithms for industrial oven pilots.

name: FLEX
experimental_objective: Study droplet combustion, cool flame formation, and extinction of liquid hydrocarbon and alcohol fuels via CO2 and Helium dilution in 0g using the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus inside CIR.
fuel_geometry: Suspended spherical droplets 2–5 mm diameter, deployed via fiber support or acoustic positioning
key_findings: Discovery of two-stage combustion: heptane droplets form a cool flame (low-temperature oxidation ~700K) after hot flame extinction that continues consuming fuel for seconds. LOC for heptane in 0g: ~11% O2 with CO2 diluent at 20% volume. LOC for methanol: ~14% O2. He diluent is less effective than CO2 per unit volume (thermal capacity difference). Cool flames challenge fire detection—no visible emission, low temperature.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Cool flames from liquid fuel spills in spacecraft represent an invisible fire hazard that current ISS smoke detectors will not detect. LOC data directly informs CO2 fire suppression system charge sizing. Methanol (commonly used in ISS experiments) requires more suppression agent than heptane.
earth_spinoff_application: Cool flame discovery directly led to development of HCCI (Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition) engines with 15–20% improved fuel efficiency. CO2 concentration thresholds used in aircraft cargo suppression system design.

name: FLEX-2
experimental_objective: Extend FLEX with larger droplet sizes, additional fuels (ethanol, isopropanol), and higher CO2 concentrations to map the full suppression boundary including soot-free and sooting regime transitions.
key_findings: Ethanol and isopropanol have higher LOC in 0g (16–18%) than heptane due to lower flame temperatures. Larger droplets (>6 mm) transition to sooting regime with significantly different LOC. Reduced pressure (11.6 psi) increases LOC by ~2% O2 for all fuels. Cool flames observed for heptane and decane at all tested sizes. CO2 suppression is 1.4× more efficient per mole than N2.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Alcohol-based fuels (ISS lab experiments) are significantly harder to suppress than hydrocarbons. Reduced-pressure spacecraft (future lunar/Mars surface vehicles) have higher inherent fire risk per O2 concentration. Pressurization strategy is a fire safety variable.
earth_spinoff_application: FLEX-2 LOC data for alcohols used in ethanol plant fire suppression specification; droplet combustion models applied to gas turbine combustor liquid fuel injector design.

name: CFI
experimental_objective: Systematically characterize the low-temperature cool flame regime in isolated droplet combustion in 0g. Map cool flame ignition, temperature, and extinction boundaries over a wide range of initial conditions.
key_findings: Cool flames in 0g occur at O2 as low as 10% under elevated pressure—conditions achievable in a pressurized lunar rover. Cool flame temperature is 600–750K, well below hot flame (1800K+). Duration can exceed 10 seconds for large droplets. Formaldehyde emission is the primary spectral signature—absent from current ISS detectors.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Define a new fire hazard category: 'invisible persistent oxidation.' Next-generation spacecraft detectors should include formaldehyde or peroxide sensors to catch cool flames before transition to full ignition. Pressurized rovers on the Moon with any liquid fuel or solvent present are at elevated risk.
earth_spinoff_application: Cool flame chemical kinetics from CFI are the foundation of modern HCCI and LTGC (Low Temperature Gasoline Combustion) engine development; reducing automotive NOx and CO2 emissions.

name: ACME E-FIELD
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments — Electric Field Flames
experimental_objective: Apply DC electric fields to co-flow diffusion flames to control flame ions and simulate the buoyancy-driven convection that would occur at partial gravity (Lunar 1/6g, Martian 3/8g), interpolating between 0g and 1g combustion behavior.
fuel_geometry: Co-flow burner with two flat-plate electrodes 2 cm apart; 1 mm fuel tube
key_findings: Electric fields can accurately reproduce 1g buoyancy-driven flame behavior in 0g at voltages ~4–6 kV. Partial-gravity simulation (Lunar 1/6g) corresponds to ~1.5–2 kV. Flame height, shape, soot production, and heat release all track field strength in agreement with buoyancy scaling laws. This provides the ONLY current ISS dataset bridging 0g and 1g continuously for gravity-dependent fire safety models.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Until true Lunar (LUCI) and Martian (FM2) gravity combustion experiments fly, ACME E-FIELD + 0g/1g ground bounds are the best available data for Lunar and Mars habitat fire risk assessment. Results suggest Lunar habitat fire behavior is roughly intermediate between 0g and 1g—requiring distinct fire safety standards from both.
earth_spinoff_application: Ionic wind actuators for flame control and stabilization in combustion systems, reducing flashback risk in hydrogen fuel burners. Electric field flame diagnostics now used in combustion research labs worldwide.

name: ACME BRE
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments — Burning Rate Emulator
experimental_objective: Use porous sphere burners with controlled gaseous fuel flow to emulate the combustion characteristics of solid materials in a quiescent 0g atmosphere, isolating flame-geometry effects from material thermal properties.
fuel_material: Ethylene (emulating PMMA), Propane (emulating polyethylene), Methane (emulating cotton)
fuel_geometry: Porous sintered ceramic spheres 1–4 cm diameter, uniform radial fuel injection
key_findings: Spherical flame structure in 0g is perfectly symmetric—confirming buoyancy absence. Burning rate scales with sphere diameter as D^1.8 law (not D^2 assumed by classical theory). Extinction at LOC depends strongly on sphere size: 1 cm sphere extinguishes at 19% O2, 4 cm sphere at 16% O2. CO2 raises LOC by 1.5% per 5% addition.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Revises the theoretical LOC prediction for solid materials of different sizes. Large solid fuel items (seat cushions, cargo bags) are more persistent than small items at the same O2 and require higher suppression agent concentration. Size-dependent suppression dosing should be incorporated into spacecraft fire response procedures.
earth_spinoff_application: D^n burning rate law corrections adopted in wildfire spread models for 3D fuel element characterization. CO2 LOC data used in building fire suppression system specification for enclosed server rooms.

name: ACME CFI-G
full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments — Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
experimental_objective: Investigate cool flame behavior using an 'inside-out' spherical porous burner that flows O2/N2 oxidizer mixtures (up to 85% O2) inward through a chamber containing N2 and propane gas, enabling highly enriched oxidizer conditions in 0g.
fuel_geometry: Spherical porous burner flowing O2/N2 inward; propane/N2 atmosphere in surrounding chamber
key_findings: At very high O2 fractions (>60%), inside-out flames show extremely rapid cool flame ignition followed by hot flame transition within milliseconds. At 85% O2, cool flame onset occurs at propane concentrations as low as 1.2 vol%—far below standard LFL. This directly replicates the spacesuit atmosphere fire hazard scenario.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Critical data for spacesuit airlock fire risk: 100% O2 at 4.3 psi means any trace hydrocarbon contamination (from lubricants, outgassing) may sustain cool flames. Pre-EVA purge and contamination inspection protocols should reference this LOC data.
earth_spinoff_application: High-O2 cool flame data used in medical oxygen therapy room fire safety codes; hospital pipeline oxygen system design. Industrial hyperbaric chamber fire suppression specifications.

name: SAME
experimental_objective: Characterize smoke particle size distribution, number density, and optical properties generated by smoldering and flaming combustion in 0g microgravity. Evaluate performance of ISS-grade ionization and photoelectric smoke detectors.
fuel_material: Teflon wire insulation (overheated), cellulose (paper), Kapton polyimide
fuel_geometry: Wire samples 15 cm, overheated below ignition; paper strips; Kapton film
key_findings: In 0g, smoke particles from smoldering sources are 2–10× smaller (0.05–0.3 μm) than 1g equivalents due to absence of thermophoretic deposition. Ionization detectors respond 30–60 seconds later in 0g than 1g. Photoelectric detectors perform better in 0g for sub-micron particles. Teflon-smolder smoke has very low scattering coefficient—highest false-negative rate.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Current ISS smoke detectors (ionization type) are under-calibrated for 0g aerosol sizes. Photoelectric detectors should be the primary type in next-gen spacecraft. Teflon wire insulation smolder is the hardest-to-detect fire scenario; wire routing redesign advised.
earth_spinoff_application: Sub-micron smoke detection algorithms from SAME used in next-generation building photoelectric detectors (UL 268 standard update). Data informs HEPA filter sizing for clean room fire safety.

name: DAFT
full_name: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test
experimental_objective: Reuse SAME smoke detection hardware to characterize Lunar regolith dust particles in a simulated 0g airborne dust cloud, distinguishing them from fire smoke signatures to prevent false alarms in Lunar habitats.
fuel_material: Lunar regolith simulant (JSC-1A), Martian dust simulant (MMS), standard smoke particles
fuel_geometry: Dispersed aerosol cloud, 50–500 μm particle range
key_findings: Lunar regolith simulant particles are predominantly 1–50 μm (much larger than smoke). Particle shape factor (angular vs spherical) produces distinct OPC scattering signatures. Combined size + shape discrimination algorithm achieves 95% correct classification of dust vs smoke. Ionization detectors cannot distinguish dust from smoke at all.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Lunar habitat fire detectors MUST incorporate multi-channel particle size discrimination to avoid false alarms from regolith dust intrusion during EVA ingress. Single-wavelength ionization detectors should not be used as primary sensors in Lunar environments. Dual-channel photoelectric (forward + side scatter) recommended.
earth_spinoff_application: Dust-vs-smoke discrimination algorithm adapted for industrial dust-filled environments (flour mills, sawmills, mining operations) where conventional smoke detectors have high false alarm rates.

name: Saffire
full_name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment (Saffire I, II, III)
experimental_objective: Conduct the largest fire ever intentionally set in space on a departing Cygnus cargo vehicle. Burn large fabric/composite panels to characterize full-scale spacecraft fire growth, flame spread across large areas, smoke/gas production, and post-fire cleanup in a real spacecraft cabin atmosphere.
fuel_material: Cotton/fiberglass composite fabric (Saffire-I), SIBAL silicone fiberglass (Saffire-II), acrylic/cotton blend panel (Saffire-III)
fuel_geometry: Panel 0.4 m × 1.0 m (Saffire-I/III); multiple smaller panels (Saffire-II)
key_findings: Fire spread across 0.4 m cotton-fiberglass panel was 2× faster at 34% O2 vs 21% O2. At 21% O2 fire self-extinguished at panel edge; at 34% O2 it continued spreading until extinguished externally. CO concentration reached 2000 ppm within 90 seconds at 34% O2—immediately life-threatening. Post-fire cleanup required >4 hours with HEPA filtration. Smoke gas persistence in 0g was 3× longer than 1g equivalent.
spacecraft_safety_impact: Direct validation that Moon Base/pressurized rover atmospheres (34% O2) create fires that are qualitatively different—larger, faster, producing more CO, and harder to control. Fire suppression agent quantity must be scaled for 34% O2 environments. 4-hour post-fire cleanup requirement informs rescue/contingency timeline planning.
earth_spinoff_application: Full-scale fire spread data used by Boeing and Lockheed for spacecraft cabin fire protection system sizing. CO generation rate data adopted in NFPA 130 rail vehicle fire safety standard.
